title: The Ascension of Jesus
lead: The risen Jesus' departure from his disciples, when he was taken up and a cloud hid him from their eyes (Acts 1:9–11; Luke 24:50–51). The creeds confess that he "ascended into heaven" and sits at the Father's right hand. The New Testament ties the ascension to Jesus' exaltation as Lord, to the sending of the Spirit and to the promise that he will come again.

sections.b: The Old Testament tells of two people God took: Enoch (Genesis 5:24) and Elijah, who went up in the windstorm while Elisha watched (2 Kings 2:11). Elijah's promise to Elisha, "If you see me being taken from you, then you will have it" (2 Kings 2:10), links seeing the departure with receiving a share of the master's spirit. The Greek Old Testament uses the same verb for Elijah, "taken up," that Luke uses for Jesus, and in Acts the disciples who watch him go receive the Spirit ten days later.
sections.refs: Genesis 5:24; 2 Kings 2:9–15; Luke 9:51; Acts 1:2; Acts 1:9–11; Acts 2:33

sections.b: For the earliest preaching the ascension is Jesus' enthronement. Peter reads Psalm 110:1 as fulfilled when Jesus was raised high at God's right hand and poured out the Spirit (Acts 2:33–35). Paul, Hebrews and 1 Peter speak of Jesus seated at God's right hand and gone into heaven (Ephesians 1:20; Hebrews 4:14; 1 Peter 3:22). John speaks of Jesus going up to the Father (John 20:17).
sections.refs: Psalm 110:1; Acts 2:33–36; Ephesians 1:20–22; Hebrews 1:3; Hebrews 4:14; 1 Peter 3:22; John 20:17

sections.b: Luke's Gospel seems to tell the ascension at the end of Easter day (Luke 24:50–51), while Acts puts it after forty days (Acts 1:3). Some explain that the Gospel compresses the story; others that Luke deliberately uses forty, the number of Moses on the mountain and of Jesus in the wilderness. Some early manuscripts of Luke 24:51 lack the words "and was carried up into heaven," a point treated in the textual notes on that verse.
